richrines · Nov 26, 2026

I’m one of the people behind Nito, a private AI platform: a chat app, plus an API and coding-agent plugins for developers. After a run of provider incidents last week, we wrote down how our setup actually works and how to check it, including the parts that aren’t perfect.

Short version: every model we serve runs in a TEE (a confidential VM plus NVIDIA confidential computing on the GPU). Encrypted requests are sealed on your device to a key the enclave proves it holds, so our gateway relays ciphertext it can’t open. The guide covers attestation step by step, what our router can still see (account, model, timing, size, token counts), and the trust model, including physical attacks like TEE.fail.

Happy to answer any/all questions

gavinray · Nov 28, 2026

Isn't this the use case that Homomorphic Encryption was practically designed for?

https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Homomorphic_encryption

  > ... a form of encryption that allows computations to be performed on encrypted data without first having to decrypt it. The result of the computations are left in an encrypted form which, when decrypted, result in an output that is identical to that of the operations performed on the unencrypted data.

teraflop · Nov 28, 2026

Well, yes, in theory. But the problem is that fully homomorphic encryption (currently) has extremely high overhead. It typically doesn't make sense to outsource a computation to somebody else if doing so is going to be 100x slower than you could perform it yourself.

This service instead uses hardware-level trusted execution. Basically that means step 1 is that the CPU/GPU performs the computation "natively", i.e. with full visibility of the plaintext, with only a small amount of overhead. Step 2 is that the hardware encrypts the output so only the intended recipient can read it. And the chip designed pinky promises that they've disabled every possible means of introspection and debugging, so that the hardware owner can't see what's happening between steps 1 and 2.
